title: Neighbours Trading Places
statement: Find the number of six-digit positive integers $N$, with non-zero leading digit, that have the following property: for each of the five pairs of adjacent digit positions of $N$, interchanging the two digits in those positions and leaving the other four digits unchanged gives a number divisible by $7$. If an interchange places a $0$ in the leading position, the result is read as an ordinary integer with that leading zero ignored.
hints: Write $N = \sum_{i=0}^{5} d_i \cdot 10^i$ and find how much the value of $N$ changes when the digits at place values $10^i$ and $10^{i+1}$ are interchanged. Look at the differences $e_i = d_i - d_{i+1}$.

Work in modular arithmetic modulo $7$. An interchange changes $N$ by $9 \cdot 10^i \cdot e_i$, where $e_i = d_i - d_{i+1}$, so each condition fixes $e_i$ as a multiple of $N$ modulo $7$. The statement does not say $7 \mid N$. To find $N$ modulo $7$, rewrite $N$ using $d_5$ and the $e_i$; the coefficients are repunits, and $7 \mid 111111$.

Substituting the values of $e_i$ into that expression for $N$ gives $N \equiv 6N \pmod 7$, so $7 \mid N$ and every $e_i$ is divisible by $7$. Hence the six digits all lie in one residue class modulo $7$, and any such number has the property. Now count these numbers class by class, taking care with the class $\{0, 7\}$, where the leading digit cannot be $0$.
solution:
Let $d_i$ be the digit at place $10^i$ and $e_i=d_i-d_{i+1}$ for $0\le i\le4$. Swapping positions $i,i+1$ gives $N+9\cdot10^i e_i$. This also holds when a $0$ reaches the front, since a leading $0$ contributes nothing.

Modulo $7$ the five conditions read $2\cdot3^i e_i\equiv -N$. Multiplying by $3\cdot5^i$ (note $6\equiv-1$, $15\equiv1$) gives $e_i\equiv 3\cdot5^i N$. So $(e_0,\dots,e_4)\equiv(3,1,5,4,6)N$.

Since $d_i=d_5+e_i+\dots+e_4$,
$$N=111111\,d_5+e_0+11e_1+111e_2+1111e_3+11111e_4.$$
Here $7\mid111111$, and $11,111,1111,11111\equiv4,6,5,2$. Hence
$$N\equiv(3+4+30+20+12)N=69N\equiv6N\pmod 7,$$
so $5N\equiv0$, i.e. $7\mid N$. Then every $e_i\equiv0$, so all six digits are congruent modulo $7$.

Conversely, if all digits are $\equiv r$, any swap keeps this, so the new number is $\equiv r\cdot111111\equiv0\pmod 7$. So the property holds exactly when all digits lie in one residue class modulo $7$.

The classes are $\{0,7\}$, $\{1,8\}$, $\{2,9\}$, and the singletons $\{3\},\{4\},\{5\},\{6\}$. Class $\{0,7\}$: the leading digit is $7$, giving $2^5=32$. Classes $\{1,8\}$ and $\{2,9\}$ give $2^6=64$ each. The singletons give $1$ each.

Total: $32+128+4=164$.
